name: United States
summary: Federal level only (states are covered separately). US residents and citizens are taxed on worldwide income. Long-term capital gains and qualified dividends are taxed at up to 20% plus the 3.8% net investment income tax, so 23.8% at the top; short-term gains and non-qualified dividends reach 40.8%. There is no federal wealth tax. Federal estate and gift tax is 40% above a unified basic exclusion of USD 15 million per person for 2026 (set permanently by the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act and indexed from 2027; portable between US-citizen spouses), and assets get a stepped-up cost basis at death. Citizenship-based taxation, PFIC rules for non-US funds and a mark-to-market exit tax for covered expatriates are structural costs.

regimes.name: US tax resident (citizen, green card holder or substantial presence)
regimes.description: Worldwide taxation at federal level; state income and estate taxes come on top depending on the state of residence.
regimes.eligibility: Citizens are always taxed; non-citizens are resident with a green card or under the substantial presence test (183 weighted days over 3 years, at least 31 in the current year). Non-citizens need an immigrant or long-stay visa (e.g. EB-5, E-2, L-1).

capital_gains.summary: Long-term gains (assets held more than 12 months) are taxed at 0%, 15% or 20%, plus 3.8% NIIT for high incomes: 23.8% at the top. For 2026 the 20% rate applies to taxable income above USD 613,700 (married filing jointly) or USD 545,500 (single). Short-term gains are ordinary income, top rate 37% (above USD 768,700 MFJ in 2026) plus 3.8% NIIT = 40.8%.
capital_gains.exemptions_thresholds: 0% LTCG rate up to USD 98,900 taxable income (MFJ, 2026). NIIT applies to net investment income above modified AGI of USD 250,000 (MFJ) / 200,000 (single), not indexed. Qualified small business stock (IRC 1202): stock acquired after 4 July 2025 excluded 50/75/100% after 3/4/5 years, cap USD 15 million.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: IRC 1(h): collectibles 28% and unrecaptured section 1250 gain 25% (plus NIIT). Capital losses offset gains plus USD 3,000 a year of ordinary income, with indefinite carry-forward. Non-US mutual funds/ETFs (UCITS) are PFICs, taxed at ordinary rates plus an interest charge unless QEF/mark-to-market elections apply. Gains on property held at death are wiped out by the step-up in basis (IRC 1014).
capital_gains.regional_differences: Most states tax capital gains as ordinary income, from 0% (e.g. Florida, Texas, Nevada) to over 10% in California and New York (plus New York City tax); Washington levies a separate tax on large long-term gains. Figures here are indicative from general knowledge, not verified in this session; the subnational file is authoritative. Puerto Rico (Act 60) is a separate territorial regime.

capital_gains.rate_basis: Top federal long-term rate 20% (IRC 1(h)) plus 3.8% NIIT (IRC 1411) = 23.8%, holding over 12 months, federal only. Foreign shares: same rate; foreign tax on the gain (rare) is creditable. Private business: 23.8% unless the QSBS exclusion applies (could be 0%). Real estate: 23.8%, but the part of the gain equal to prior depreciation is taxed at 25% + 3.8%. Individual shares/US ETFs assumed; non-US funds are PFICs and are worse.
capital_gains.professional_trader: Trader status (IRC 475(f) mark-to-market election) converts gains to ordinary income; investors are not recharacterised merely by volume. Short holding periods (12 months or less) mean ordinary rates up to 37% + 3.8%.
capital_gains.holding_period_rules: More than 12 months for long-term rates.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed; foreign tax credit (IRC 901) for foreign tax paid. Exit tax for covered expatriates: deemed sale of all assets the day before expatriation, first USD 910,000 of gain excluded (2026).

dividends.summary: Qualified dividends (from US companies and from foreign companies in treaty countries or listed in the US, holding period met) are taxed at the long-term capital gains rates: up to 20% plus 3.8% NIIT = 23.8%. Non-qualified dividends (e.g. from non-treaty-country companies, PFICs) are ordinary income at up to 37% + 3.8% = 40.8%. Foreign withholding tax is credited.
dividends.exemptions_thresholds: Same 0%/15%/20% bands as capital gains (2026 MFJ: 0% to USD 98,900, 20% above USD 613,700). NIIT above USD 250,000 MAGI (MFJ).
dividends.important_exceptions: A foreign corporation's dividend is qualified only if the company is eligible for a comprehensive US treaty or the shares are readily tradable on a US exchange, and it is not a PFIC. Holding period: more than 60 days in the 121-day window around the ex-date.
dividends.regional_differences: States tax dividends as ordinary income (0% to over 10%, plus local taxes such as New York City); see the subnational file.
dividends.rate_basis: Qualified dividend rate 20% + 3.8% NIIT = 23.8% for a top-bracket family, federal only. Foreign dividends from treaty-country companies are qualified; typical 15% treaty WHT is credited against the 23.8%, so the total stays about 23.8%.
dividends.withholding_outbound: 30% statutory WHT on US-source dividends paid to foreign persons, reduced by treaty (typically 15%, 5% for qualifying corporate parents).
dividends.treaty_network: About 56 income tax treaties in force (PwC table; Hungary terminated from 2024, Russia suspended). Every US treaty contains a saving clause letting the US tax its citizens and residents as if the treaty did not exist.
dividends.holding_company_notes: C corporations pay 21% federal CIT and distributions are taxed again at 23.8%. A closely held investment company (more than 50% by value owned by 5 or fewer individuals, at least 60% of adjusted ordinary gross income from dividends, interest and similar passive income) is a personal holding company and pays an extra 20% tax on undistributed income (IRC 541-542); the 20% accumulated earnings tax (IRC 531) catches profits retained beyond business needs. A C corporation therefore cannot shelter a portfolio. Most US family offices use LLCs taxed as partnerships (transparent). The useful structure is an irrevocable GST-exempt dynasty trust taxed as a grantor trust, modelled as the 'dynasty_trust' structure regime.

wealth_tax.regional_differences: No state currently levies a broad net wealth tax. Local property taxes on real estate are significant and vary widely (not quantified here).
wealth_tax.property_tax_note: No federal property tax; states and localities tax real property (and some tax personal property). A few states historically taxed intangibles.

inheritance.summary: Federal estate tax is levied on the estate at 40% on the taxable estate above the basic exclusion amount, USD 15,000,000 per person for deaths in 2026 (OBBBA made the higher exclusion permanent and indexes it from 2027). Gift and estate tax are unified: lifetime gifts above the USD 19,000 per-recipient annual exclusion use up the same USD 15 million. Unused exclusion of a deceased spouse is portable, so a married couple shelters USD 30 million. Assets get a step-up in cost basis at death, eliminating the embedded capital gain. Scored for a married couple using portability (IRC 2010(c)(2)(B), deceased spousal unused exclusion): the second estate can shelter USD 30,000,000 (2 x USD 15,000,000) if a timely Form 706 portability election is made at the first death.
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Basic exclusion USD 15,000,000 per decedent (2026); annual gift exclusion USD 19,000 per donee (USD 38,000 with gift-splitting); unlimited marital deduction for a US-citizen spouse; gifts to a non-citizen spouse USD 194,000 a year (2026). GST tax exemption equals the basic exclusion.
inheritance.important_exceptions: The marital deduction for a non-citizen surviving spouse requires a qualified domestic trust (QDOT). Non-resident non-citizens: estate tax on US-situs assets (including US shares) with a filing threshold of only USD 60,000 (not indexed). Gifts or bequests received by US persons from covered expatriates are taxed to the recipient at the top rate (IRC 2801).
inheritance.regional_differences: About a dozen states and DC levy estate taxes and a few levy inheritance taxes (not verified in this session; see the subnational file). Probate costs vary by state and are usually avoided with a revocable living trust.

inheritance.spouse_note: Unlimited marital deduction for property passing to a surviving spouse (IRC 2056(a)), but only if the spouse is a US citizen or the property goes into a qualified domestic trust (2056(d)); it defers the tax, since the assets are in the survivor's estate (the unused exclusion is portable).
inheritance.gift_tax: Unified with the estate tax: 40% on lifetime gifts above the USD 19,000 annual exclusion once the USD 15 million lifetime exclusion is used; paid by the donor.
inheritance.business_relief: No exemption for business assets; IRC 6166 allows deferral of estate tax on closely held business interests over up to 14 years, and IRC 2032A special-use valuation for farms/businesses.
inheritance.foreign_assets: US citizens and US-domiciled non-citizens: worldwide estate. Non-domiciled non-citizens: US-situs assets only (US real estate, shares of US companies, tangible property in the US).
inheritance.domicile_rules: Estate tax uses domicile (living in the US with intent to remain), not the income tax residence test. Green card holders are usually domiciled. Expatriates who are covered expatriates trigger the IRC 2801 recipient tax on later gifts/bequests to US persons.

regimes.name: Irrevocable GST-exempt dynasty trust taxed as a grantor trust
regimes.description: The parents each give up to their USD 15 million gift/estate exclusion (USD 30 million for a couple) to an irrevocable trust for the children and later generations, allocating the equal GST exemption so the trust is never subject to estate or generation-skipping tax. The trust is drafted as a grantor trust (e.g. a power to swap assets), so the parents keep paying the income tax on its gains and dividends at their own rates; those payments shrink their taxable estate without counting as further gifts. Assets in the trust and all their later growth pass outside the parents' taxable estates. Federal layer only; state income and estate taxes are not reflected in this regime.
regimes.eligibility: Donors must be US citizens or US-domiciled non-citizens to use the USD 15 million exclusion (non-domiciled non-citizens have no lifetime gift exclusion). The parents must give up control and benefit: they cannot be beneficiaries (except a spouse in a spousal lifetime access trust) or hold powers that pull the assets back into their estates (IRC 2036/2038). Perpetual duration requires a trust governed by the law of a state that has abolished or extended the rule against perpetuities (e.g. South Dakota, Nevada, Delaware). Gift-splitting needs both spouses to be citizens or residents.
regimes.duration_note: No federal time limit: the GST exemption allocated when the trust is funded protects the trust permanently, and in states without a rule against perpetuities the trust can last indefinitely. Grantor-trust status ends at the grantor's death or when the power is released; the trust then pays its own income tax (see exit_and_liquidation).

structure.entity: Irrevocable dynasty trust (intentionally defective grantor trust), usually a directed trust sitused in a no-perpetuities state
structure.payout_notes: Distributions of trust capital or income to the children are not taxable to them while the trust is a grantor trust: the parents already pay the tax on all trust income (IRC 671 ff.). The parents themselves cannot receive distributions without bringing the assets back into their estates, so the family's own spending must come from assets kept outside the trust (a spousal lifetime access trust lets one spouse benefit, at the cost of using only the other spouse's exclusion). After grantor status ends, a non-grantor trust is taxed at trust rates (ordinary income at 37% above USD 16,000 and long-term gains at 20% above USD 16,250 in 2026, Rev. Proc. 2025-32, plus 3.8% NIIT) unless it distributes income, which is then taxed to the beneficiaries.
structure.substance_and_anti_avoidance: Running cost is a rough estimate (administrative or directed trustee fee, trust accounting and information returns, legal review), not sourced; investment management is assumed to stay with the family office. Grantor-trust rules: IRC 671-679 (a substitution power under IRC 675(4)(C) is the usual trigger). Estate inclusion risks: retained interests or control (IRC 2036, 2038), the reciprocal-trust doctrine for mirror-image spousal trusts, and implied agreements to benefit the grantor. The grantor's payment of the trust's income tax is not treated as a gift (Rev. Rul. 2004-64; not opened in this session). Trust assets get no step-up in basis at the grantor's death (Rev. Rul. 2023-2), so the children inherit the parents' cost basis and pay up to 23.8% when they sell, unless low-basis assets are swapped back to the grantor before death. State law matters: the trust's situs state determines perpetual duration and whether a non-grantor trust pays state income tax; Connecticut has a gift tax and some estate-tax states (e.g. New York) add back recent gifts. C-corporation alternatives are penalised: a personal holding company tax of 20% on undistributed passive income (IRC 541-542) and a 20% accumulated earnings tax (IRC 531) apply on top of 21% CIT.
structure.exit_and_liquidation: Emigration of the grantor: a covered expatriate faces the IRC 877A mark-to-market exit tax on assets he or she is treated as owning (grantor-trust assets included, per the IRS expatriation rules; not verified in detail), and later distributions to US beneficiaries of covered gifts can be hit by IRC 2801. Moving the trust's trustee or control abroad makes it a foreign trust and can trigger tax on unrealised gains (IRC 684; not verified). Terminating or distributing the trust is not an estate-tax event once GST exemption covers it; distributed assets keep their carryover basis.

capital_gains.summary: While the trust is a grantor trust, all its gains are taxed to the parents as if they held the assets directly: long-term gains at up to 20% plus 3.8% NIIT = 23.8%, short-term gains as ordinary income up to 40.8%. The trust itself pays nothing.
capital_gains.rate_basis: Grantor trust: income and gains are reported by the grantor (IRC 671). Rates are the standard federal individual rates: 20% + 3.8% NIIT for gains on assets held more than 12 months. Federal only. The price of the structure is the lost step-up at death (Rev. Rul. 2023-2), which is not a rate here.
capital_gains.important_exceptions: Assets in the trust do not get a stepped-up basis at the grantor's death (Rev. Rul. 2023-2): the embedded gain stays taxable to the trust or children on a later sale. Once grantor status ends, gains retained in the trust are taxed at trust rates (top 20% + 3.8% NIIT, reached at very low income).
capital_gains.professional_trader: As standard: trader status or short holding periods mean ordinary rates up to 37% + 3.8%.
capital_gains.foreign_assets: Worldwide gains taxed to the grantor with a foreign tax credit, as for direct holding.

dividends.summary: Dividends earned by a grantor trust are taxed to the parents as their own: qualified dividends at up to 23.8% including NIIT, with credit for foreign withholding tax.
dividends.rate_basis: Grantor trust: same as direct holding, 20% qualified dividend rate + 3.8% NIIT = 23.8%; treaty WHT (typically 15%) credited. Federal only.
dividends.holding_company_notes: The trust is a pass-through for income tax while grantor status lasts; it pays no tax of its own.

inheritance.summary: Assets given to the trust (up to the donors' USD 15 million exclusion each in 2026, USD 30 million for a couple) and all their later growth are outside the parents' taxable estates and, with GST exemption allocated, outside the children's and grandchildren's estates as well. Only assets kept outside the trust bear the 40% estate tax at death. Modelled as an estate-basis tax with a USD 30 million exemption: both parents fund the trust during life with their full exclusions; the remaining estate is taxed at 40%.
inheritance.spouse_note: Unlimited marital deduction for property passing to a surviving spouse (IRC 2056(a)), but only if the spouse is a US citizen or the property goes into a qualified domestic trust (2056(d)); it defers the tax, since the assets are in the survivor's estate (the unused exclusion is portable).
inheritance.exemptions_thresholds: Basic exclusion USD 15,000,000 per donor for 2026 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32), indexed from 2027; GST exemption equals the basic exclusion (IRC 2631(c)). Annual exclusion gifts (USD 19,000 per donee) can also fund the trust, but need Crummey powers and do not carry GST exemption automatically.
inheritance.important_exceptions: The static figure understates the benefit and overstates the difference to direct holding in one respect. Understates: growth after funding escapes estate tax entirely (a USD 30 million trust growing at 5% a year is worth about USD 80 million after 20 years, all outside the estate), and the grantor's income-tax payments further shrink the taxable estate. Overstates: the standard regime in this file counts one USD 15 million exclusion, while a married couple can in principle shelter USD 30 million on death too through portability (with QDOT requirements when the surviving spouse is not a citizen). The cost: no basis step-up for trust assets (Rev. Rul. 2023-2), so up to 23.8% on embedded gains when the children sell. State estate or gift taxes are not reflected.
inheritance.gift_tax: Funding the trust is a taxable gift that uses the donor's lifetime exclusion (USD 15 million in 2026); above it, 40% gift tax paid by the donor. A gift tax return (Form 709) allocating GST exemption is required.
inheritance.business_relief: None specific to the trust; private-company stakes are often given at valuation discounts for lack of control and marketability (not modelled).
inheritance.foreign_assets: Worldwide assets can be placed in the trust; the donor must be a US citizen or domiciliary to use the USD 15 million exclusion.
inheritance.domicile_rules: As for the standard regime: estate and gift tax follow citizenship or domicile. Trust assets remain outside the estate even if the parents later leave the US, but a covered expatriate's later gifts to US persons are taxed under IRC 2801.

residency.tax_residency_test: Income tax: citizens always; non-citizens with a green card (lawful permanent residents) or meeting the substantial presence test (at least 31 days in the year and 183 days counting all current-year days, 1/3 of prior-year days and 1/6 of the second prior year), subject to the closer-connection exception. Estate tax: domicile. Leaving after holding a green card in 8 of the last 15 years (long-term resident) or renouncing citizenship triggers the IRC 877A exit tax for covered expatriates (net worth USD 2 million or more, average net income tax above USD 211,000 for 2026, or failure to certify compliance).

routes.name: EB-5 immigrant investor (green card)
routes.requirements: Investment in a qualifying US commercial enterprise creating 10 jobs; the statutory amounts (USD 1,050,000, or USD 800,000 in a targeted employment area) were not verified in this session. Gives permanent residence for the family and full US tax residence.

routes.name: E-2 treaty investor / L-1 / O-1 visas
routes.requirements: Non-immigrant routes; E-2 is available only to nationals of treaty countries. Not verified in detail.

corporate.summary: Flat 21% federal CIT plus state CIT of roughly 1-10% (some states none). 15% corporate alternative minimum tax for corporations with average financial statement income above USD 1 billion. Dividends paid by a C corporation are taxed again at shareholder level (23.8%), so families usually hold investments directly or through pass-through LLCs/partnerships.
corporate.special_zones: Opportunity zones (deferral/exclusion of reinvested gains) and state-level incentives; not modelled.

sources.title: United States - Corporate - Taxes on corporate income

us_citizen_notes: This file is the US federal layer itself. US citizens are taxed on worldwide income and estates wherever they live; the app adds this layer to other countries. Renouncing citizenship triggers the IRC 877A exit tax for covered expatriates (deemed sale, USD 910,000 exclusion for 2026).
open_questions: State taxes are deliberately excluded (covered by the subnational file).
EB-5 investment amounts and visa routes not verified in this session.
Cost of living omitted: it depends entirely on the state/city, which the subnational research covers.
Whether the US Pillar Two 'side-by-side' arrangement affects family holding companies was not researched (it concerns large multinationals).

prime_rent_monthly.description: Median asking rent of 10 four-bedroom houses to let in family areas of Austin on Zumper, read 2026-10-15 from all four pages (192 results) of the Austin 4-bedroom house search, keeping only family districts and dropping the University of Texas student-house belt (West University, Hancock, North University, Hyde Park, North Loop). Listings: Circle C (3: USD 3,800, 3,945, 4,100), Westlake/Barton Hills area ZIP 78746 (2: USD 6,894, 7,495), Mueller (USD 5,000), Wooten (USD 6,900), North Shoal Creek (USD 3,600), ZIP 78730 northwest (USD 2,750) and South River City (USD 6,800). Range USD 2,750-7,495; most listings do not state floor area, those that do are 1,784-3,068 sq ft (about 165-285 m2). Tarrytown and Allandale had no 4-bedroom house listed. Base rent; fees may apply.

cost_of_living.notes: Austin, TX (upper-middle-class benchmark, replacing New York). Prime price per m2, family health insurance and housekeeper not sourced and omitted. The rent sample is skewed by student-oriented houses near the University of Texas; the median is a central-Austin figure, not a Tarrytown or Westlake figure.
